title: Songs, sharks and Charlie Kirk: Commemorative bills are many, but few are passed into law
summary: It's a rite of Annapolis. Every year Maryland legislators hear requests for commemorative pieces of legislation and official state symbols, but even though "the testimony is compelling," few end up making the cut, even after repeated tries.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 16, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 16, 2026

There’s little doubt that 9-year-old Preston Milloy’s pitch to make the Natural History Society of Maryland the state’s official natural history museum was sincere.

Preston traveled with his parents from Baltimore County to testify Thursday before the Senate Education, Energy and the Environment Committee in support of Senate Bill 35, which would do just that. He told committee members that he’s a member of the museum, where he has participated in various events, such as telling visitors about his love of reptiles and his pet snake that he named “Pizza.”

“At the NHS, I am seen and respected. It doesn’t matter that I’m a kid,” Preston said from prepared remarks. “It’s a great museum run by great people, but it’s not recognized enough. I want people to love, protect, and most importantly, respect wildlife.”

It was a good pitch, and heartfelt. Unfortunately for Preston, and the supporters of a dozen other bills to designate an official state this or that, the Maryland General Assembly’s one and only requirement during the 90-day legislative session is to approve a balanced budget.

It’s not hopeless: Lawmakers last year designated chromite as the official state mineral, but that took eight years to win passage. Meanwhile, advocates like Preston keep making their cases.

This is at least the third go-round for Preston’s bill, a House version of which is sehcduled to be heard Monday by the Government, Labor and Elections Committee.

Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) hopes “the third time’s the charm” for Senate Bill 627, the bill he presented to the committee Thursday to make Jan. 13 “Korean American Day,” the day Korean migrants arrived to the United States in 1903. A House version sponsored by Del. Courtney Watson (D-Howard) is set to be heard Tuesday by Government, Labor and Elections.

While few of the bills calling for new official state symbols or official designations will ever make it out of committee, much less into law, their annual appearance on the committees’ calendars often generate smiles and a standing ovation. And little known facts about the state, like the megalodon.

Zoey Godfrey, 9, and Harper Coale, 11, came before the Education, Energy and Environment Committee to urge Maryland to designate the prehistoric megalodon as the state’s shark.

Zoey held a poster of the megalodon (formerly called “Otodus megalodon”), while Harper spoke in support of Senate Bill 135 sponsored by Sen. Jack Bailey (R-Calvert and St. Mary’s).

Harper said the megalodon teeth have been found in Maryland along the Chesapeake Bay and Calvert Cliffs State Park in Calvert County.

“Even though the megalodon is extinct, worrying about it today can help people understand the ocean’s ecosystem and the role sharks play in our nature today,” Harper said.

Zoey’s father, Stephen Godfrey, curator of paleontology at the Calvert Marine Museum in Calvert County, said the megalodon stretched nearly 80 feet and its fossilized teeth have been found in seven Maryland counties. Godfrey provided committee members with sets of megalodon teeth in plastic bags with a piece of paper inside: “Genuine Megalodon Tooth? Maryland State Shark?”

According to the museum, no other state in the nation has ever made that designation. If approved, Maryland would become the first.

“I never thought I would be popular in science. I actually got there by sponsoring a bill,” Bailey said.

Bailey received plenty of support from fourth-grade students at Beltsville Academy in Prince George’s County, who submitted persuasive letters and drawings of the megalodon.

Anna Shay, 22, a fourth-grade teacher at the academy, said in an interview Friday that one of her students’ parents informed her about the proposed legislation. Shay, with help from her fourth-grade team and an English-language-learner teacher, transformed the lesson into a writing, science and social studies project.

“Even if it doesn’t pass, the experience they had is being able to write a persuasive letter and being involved in the legislative process,” Shay said. “At the end of the day, their voices matter. I listened to them. Their government listened to them. They have so much value in this world.”

The House version sponsored by Del. Todd Morgan (R-Calvert and St. Mary’s) is scheduled to be heard Tuesday.

Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Senate Education, Energy and the Environment Committee, acknowledged Friday his committee experienced a first during this four-year legislative term.

Jayla Elise, who turned 23 on Saturday, used her two minutes of testimony to sing to the committee. More specifically, she sang in support of Senate Bill 191 to make “The Heart of Maryland,” which Elise also wrote, the state song.

“I wanted this song to reflect where we’ve been and where we’re going,” Elise, who currently resides in Cambridge, told the committee.

A post shared by William Ford (@jabariwill2809)

Here’s a few of the lyrics: “Together, we stand in the heart of this land, Through steel and stone, we call this place home, Where the history lives and the families thrive, Maryland’s spirit stays alive.”

The bill’s sponsor, Sen. Benjamin Brooks (D-Baltimore County), said the previous state song, “Maryland, My Maryland” doesn’t represent the state’s inclusiveness today.

The legislature voted to repeal “Maryland, My Maryland” as the state song in 2021. Opponents noted that it was composed during the Civil War by a Confederate sympathizer, James Ryder Randall, and made a state symbol in 1939 during racial tensions.

“This is what I would call a feel-good song that’s representative of all of us,” Brooks said after Thursday’s hearings. “You’ve got a 22-year-old Black woman who wrote a song for the state that brings that kind of feeling, that kind of humanity, that kind of togetherness for the entire state.”

The Maryland 250 Commission, which the governor created through an executive order in 2023 to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary in July, supports the song. One of its members, Patricia Maclay, a physician with a background in neuroscience, said the song can help boosts a person’s mood, lower the heart rate and “foster greater social connection.”

Katie Curran O’Malley, a retired Baltimore City judge and vice chair of the commission, said Maryland and New Jersey are the only two states without a state song.

“Maryland needs a state song, and I can’t think of anything more appropriate than Jayla Elise’s ‘The Heart of Maryland,’” O’Malley said.

There’s a few more requests for state designations and resolutions scheduled to be heard this week, including:

Feldman, chair of Education, Energy and Environment Committee, said Friday his committee had another first last month when there was a dog at the witness table during a hearing on a bill dealing with therapy dogs at public schools. Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) serves as the lead sponsor.

“We’re breaking new ground in the Triple-E Committee,” Feldman said.

But Feldman acknowledged there’s some resistance passing too many commemorative pieces of legislation.

“It’s hard because the testimony is compelling, and you would like to pass them all, but then we would have hundreds of pages of commemorative days and designation days,” he said.

“We’ll continue to be very thoughtful and judicious about what kinds of commemorative days we do,” Feldman said. “I think this year you’re just going to see a few come out of the House and a few from the Senate.”

— This story was corrected on Monday, March 16, to correct the sponsor of the House megalodon bill. It is Del. Todd Morgan (R-St. Mary’s and Calvert).
